claim: COMPASS mutations reduce replicative lifespan in budding yeast.
source: We find that COMPASS mutations reduce replicative lifespan and cause expression defects in almost 500 genes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced viability in COMPASS mutants across aging time points.

claim: COMPASS mutations cause expression defects in almost 500 genes.
source: We find that COMPASS mutations reduce replicative lifespan and cause expression defects in almost 500 genes.
evidence: Supported by mRNAseq data showing differential expression in COMPASS mutants.

claim: H3K4 methylation acts primarily in gene repression, particularly in yeast.
source: Although H3K4 methylation is reported to act primarily in gene repression, particularly in yeast, repressive functions are progressively lost with age while hundreds of genes become dependent on H3K4me3 for full expression.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on H3K4 methylation function.

claim: Repressive functions of H3K4 methylation are progressively lost with age.
source: Although H3K4 methylation is reported to act primarily in gene repression, particularly in yeast, repressive functions are progressively lost with age while hundreds of genes become dependent on H3K4me3 for full expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing gene expression in COMPASS mutants across aging time points.

claim: Hundreds of genes become dependent on H3K4me3 for full expression during aging.
source: Although H3K4 methylation is reported to act primarily in gene repression, particularly in yeast, repressive functions are progressively lost with age while hundreds of genes become dependent on H3K4me3 for full expression.
evidence: Supported by mRNAseq data showing under-expression of genes in COMPASS mutants at 48 hours.

claim: Basal and inducible expression of H3K4me3-dependent genes is impaired in young cells lacking COMPASS components Swd1 or Spp1.
source: Basal and inducible expression of these genes is also impaired in young cells lacking COMPASS components Swd1 or Spp1.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data showing reduced BNA gene expression in swd1Δ and spp1Δ mutants.

claim: Gene induction during ageing is associated with increasing promoter H3K4me3.
source: Gene induction during ageing is associated with increasing promoter H3K4me3, but H3K4me3 also accumulates in non-promoter regions and the ribosomal DNA.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data showing correlation between gene induction and H3K4me3 changes.

claim: H3K4me3 accumulates in non-promoter regions during aging.
source: Gene induction during ageing is associated with increasing promoter H3K4me3, but H3K4me3 also accumulates in non-promoter regions and the ribosomal DNA.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data showing H3K4me3 distribution changes with age.

claim: H3K4me3 accumulates in the ribosomal DNA during aging.
source: Gene induction during ageing is associated with increasing promoter H3K4me3, but H3K4me3 also accumulates in non-promoter regions and the ribosomal DNA.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data showing increased H3K4me3 in rDNA regions.

claim: H3K4me3 is required to maintain normal expression of many genes across organismal lifespan.
source: Our results provide clear evidence that H3K4me3 is required to maintain normal expression of many genes across organismal lifespan.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing gene expression defects in COMPASS mutants across aging.

claim: H3K4me3 is ubiquitously observed on nucleosomes at the 5' end of eukaryotic genes undergoing active transcription by RNA polymerase II.
source: H3K4me3 is ubiquitously observed on nucleosomes at the 5' end of eukaryotic genes undergoing active transcription by RNA polymerase II (see for example [Barski et al., 2007; Bernstein et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2009]).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing H3K4me3 localization.

claim: The tight correlation between promoter H3K4me3 and transcriptional activity has led to H3K4me3 being widely considered as an activating mark.
source: The tight correlation between promoter H3K4me3 and transcriptional activity has led to H3K4me3 being widely considered as an activating mark, however, direct evidence for a role in steady-state transcription or gene induction is rare and controversial (reviewed in [Howe et al., 2017]).
evidence: Supported by citation to review discussing the controversy.

claim: Direct evidence for a role of H3K4me3 in steady-state transcription or gene induction is rare and controversial.
source: The tight correlation between promoter H3K4me3 and transcriptional activity has led to H3K4me3 being widely considered as an activating mark, however, direct evidence for a role in steady-state transcription or gene induction is rare and controversial (reviewed in [Howe et al., 2017]).
evidence: Supported by citation to review discussing the controversy.

claim: H3K4me3 is primarily deposited by the highly conserved COMPASS complexes.
source: H3K4me3 is primarily deposited by the highly conserved COMPASS complexes (Briggs et al., 2001; Krogan et al., 2002; Miller et al., 2001; Roguev et al., 2001; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies identifying COMPASS as the H3K4 methyltransferase.

claim: Budding yeast has a single COMPASS complex containing the catalytic SET-domain protein Set1 and core structural proteins Swd1 and Swd3, along with Sdc1, Bre2, Swd2 and Spp1.
source: Budding yeast has a single COMPASS complex containing the catalytic SET-domain protein Set1 and core structural proteins Swd1 and Swd3, along with Sdc1, Bre2, Swd2 and Spp1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of COMPASS composition and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Set1, Swd1 and Swd3 are required for all H3K4 methylation activity.
source: Set1, Swd1 and Swd3 are required for all H3K4 methylation activity, while Sdc1 and Bre2 are necessary for di- and tri-methylation (Dehé et al., 2006; Schneider et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing COMPASS component functions.

claim: Sdc1 and Bre2 are necessary for H3K4 di- and tri-methylation.
source: Set1, Swd1 and Swd3 are required for all H3K4 methylation activity, while Sdc1 and Bre2 are necessary for di- and tri-methylation (Dehé et al., 2006; Schneider et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing COMPASS component functions.

claim: Neither Swd2 nor Spp1 are required for H3K4 methylation in vitro.
source: Neither Swd2 nor Spp1 are required for H3K4 methylation in vitro (Takahashi et al., 2011), but mutation of Swd2 almost completely abrogates H3K4me3 and reduces H3K4me2 in vivo (Cheng et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2007), while loss of Spp1 dramatically reduces H3K4me3 in vivo without impacting H3K4me1/2 (Dehé et al., 2006; Schneider et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: Mutation of Swd2 almost completely abrogates H3K4me3 and reduces H3K4me2 in vivo.
source: Neither Swd2 nor Spp1 are required for H3K4 methylation in vitro (Takahashi et al., 2011), but mutation of Swd2 almost completely abrogates H3K4me3 and reduces H3K4me2 in vivo (Cheng et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2007), while loss of Spp1 dramatically reduces H3K4me3 in vivo without impacting H3K4me1/2 (Dehé et al., 2006; Schneider et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to in vivo studies.

claim: Loss of Spp1 dramatically reduces H3K4me3 in vivo without impacting H3K4me1/2.
source: Neither Swd2 nor Spp1 are required for H3K4 methylation in vitro (Takahashi et al., 2011), but mutation of Swd2 almost completely abrogates H3K4me3 and reduces H3K4me2 in vivo (Cheng et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2007), while loss of Spp1 dramatically reduces H3K4me3 in vivo without impacting H3K4me1/2 (Dehé et al., 2006; Schneider et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to in vivo studies.

claim: Cells lacking COMPASS components Swd1 or Swd3 have replicative lifespans approximately 20% shorter than wild type.
source: A published micromanipulation screen of 264 yeast mutants found that cells lacking COMPASS components Swd1 or Swd3 have replicative lifespans ~ 20% shorter than wild type (Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published screen.

claim: MEP swd1Δ cells show a substantial and significant defect in replicative lifespan, being only approximately 50% viable at 24 hr and almost completely inviable after 48 hr in YPD.
source: As expected, MEP swd1Δ cells show a substantial and significant defect in replicative lifespan, being only ~50% viable at 24 hr and almost completely inviable after 48 hr in YPD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The lifespan defect in swd1Δ mutants was recapitulated in catalytic dead set1H1017L and H3K4me3-defective spp1Δ mutants.
source: Importantly, this lifespan defect was recapitulated in catalytic dead set1H1017L and H3K4me3-defective spp1Δ mutants, showing that the lifespan defect results specifically from loss of H3K4me3 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by viability data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The lifespan defect in COMPASS mutants results specifically from loss of H3K4me3.
source: Importantly, this lifespan defect was recapitulated in catalytic dead set1H1017L and H3K4me3-defective spp1Δ mutants, showing that the lifespan defect results specifically from loss of H3K4me3 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of viability across different COMPASS mutants.

claim: Viability of H3K4A and H3K4R mutants was substantially and significantly reduced compared to wild-type at 24 hr.
source: Selection against daughter cells is imperfect in haploid MEPs (Lindstrom and Gottschling, 2009), a problem that can be partially offset by measuring viability at 24 hr, and at this point we observed that viability of the mutants was substantially and significantly reduced compared to the wild-type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: COMPASS mutants have a reduced chronological lifespan due to stimulation of apoptosis by the H3K79 methyltransferase Dot1.
source: COMPASS mutants also have a reduced chronological lifespan due to stimulation of apoptosis by the H3K79 methyltransferase Dot1 (Walter et al., 2014); however no suppression of the replicative lifespan defect was observed in swd1Δ dot1Δ double mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) so the replicative and chronological lifespan defects cannot be attributed to the same mechanism.
evidence: Supported by citation and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The replicative and chronological lifespan defects in COMPASS mutants cannot be attributed to the same mechanism.
source: COMPASS mutants also have a reduced chronological lifespan due to stimulation of apoptosis by the H3K79 methyltransferase Dot1 (Walter et al., 2014); however no suppression of the replicative lifespan defect was observed in swd1Δ dot1Δ double mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) so the replicative and chronological lifespan defects cannot be attributed to the same mechanism.
evidence: Supported by data showing no suppression in double mutants.

claim: H3K4me3 has a prominent function in ageing cells.
source: Overall, although spp1Δ mutants have a very weak phenotype during normal growth, this mutation dramatically impairs lifespan as do all tested mutants that impact H3K4 methylation, indicating that H3K4me3 has a prominent function in ageing cells.
evidence: Inferred from the dramatic lifespan defects observed in H3K4 methylation mutants.

claim: PC1, representing 49% of variance in the mRNAseq dataset, corresponds to age.
source: Principle component (PC) analysis of this dataset shows that PC1, 49% of variance, corresponds to age with both wild type and COMPASS mutant samples of equivalent ages having similar PC1 values (Figure 1C), although the log and 7.5 hr samples are similar and do not segregate well.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PC2, representing 6% of variance in the mRNAseq dataset, broadly segregates wild type from COMPASS mutant libraries.
source: PC2, 6% of variance, broadly segregates wild type from COMPASS mutant libraries (Figure 1C, note that wild type samples in blue/green lie towards the top whilst COMPASS mutants in yellow/red are largely in the lower half).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The gene expression phenotype caused by COMPASS mutation is separable from the gene expression phenotype caused by ageing.
source: The small effect of COMPASS genotype is not unexpected given previous reports, but shows that the gene expression phenotype caused by COMPASS mutation is separable from the gene expression phenotype caused by ageing.
evidence: Inferred from the PCA analysis showing distinct contributions of age and genotype.

claim: 2842 out of 6662 annotated open reading frames differ significantly between log and 48 hr in wild-type.
source: Differential expression analysis of the wild-type dataset identified 2842 out of 6662 annotated open reading frames (ORFs) that differ significantly between log and 48 hr, with very similar results in the swd1Δ mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Translation-associated terms are down-regulated relative to average with age.
source: GO analysis of these ORFs confirmed many previous findings: translation-associated terms are down-regulated relative to average with age (Hu et al., 2014; Janssens et al., 2015; Kamei et al., 2014; Yiu et al., 2008), while cell wall organisation, hexose transport, sporulation, tricarboxylic acid cycle and DNA integration (i.e. transposon activity) are upregulated as variously reported (Hu et al., 2014; Kamei et al., 2014; Koc et al., 2004; Lesur and Campbell, 2004).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: Cell wall organisation, hexose transport, sporulation, tricarboxylic acid cycle and DNA integration are upregulated with age.
source: GO analysis of these ORFs confirmed many previous findings: translation-associated terms are down-regulated relative to average with age (Hu et al., 2014; Janssens et al., 2015; Kamei et al., 2014; Yiu et al., 2008), while cell wall organisation, hexose transport, sporulation, tricarboxylic acid cycle and DNA integration (i.e. transposon activity) are upregulated as variously reported (Hu et al., 2014; Kamei et al., 2014; Koc et al., 2004; Lesur and Campbell, 2004).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: Genes upregulated with age are generally expressed at low levels in young cells.
source: Genes upregulated with age are generally expressed at low levels in young cells, while genes that are highly expressed in young cells tend to be down-regulated with age relative to average as previously observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B)(Hu et al., 2014); in absolute terms, it has been shown that all yeast genes are actually induced to a greater or lesser extent during ageing, and we therefore refer to all gene expression changes as relative to average (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and citation.

claim: All yeast genes are actually induced to a greater or lesser extent during ageing in absolute terms.
source: Genes upregulated with age are generally expressed at low levels in young cells, while genes that are highly expressed in young cells tend to be down-regulated with age relative to average as previously observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B)(Hu et al., 2014); in absolute terms, it has been shown that all yeast genes are actually induced to a greater or lesser extent during ageing, and we therefore refer to all gene expression changes as relative to average (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: There is a strong correlation between age-linked gene expression and changes following histone H3 depletion.
source: Age-related gene induction has been directly attributed to loss of histones, and we observe a strong correlation between age-linked gene expression and previously described changes following histone H3 depletion (Figure 1D)(Gossett and Lieb, 2012; Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D and citations.

claim: 204 genes are robustly upregulated during ageing but not on H3 depletion, enriched for cell wall organization functions.
source: This left a core set of 204 genes, enriched for cell wall organization functions, that are robustly upregulated during ageing but not on H3 depletion (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by filtering analysis and GO enrichment shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 13% of genes upregulated during ageing but not on H3 depletion are significantly under-expressed in the swd1Δ mutant at 48 hr but not at log phase.
source: Remarkably, 13% of these genes are significantly under-expressed in the swd1Δ mutant at 48 hr but not at log phase (Figure 1F), and also under-expressed in set1H1017L and spp1Δ mutants (data not shown), suggesting that cryptic functions for H3K4 methylation in facilitating gene expression are unmasked during the widespread gene induction that accompanies ageing.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cryptic functions for H3K4 methylation in facilitating gene expression are unmasked during the widespread gene induction that accompanies ageing.
source: Remarkably, 13% of these genes are significantly under-expressed in the swd1Δ mutant at 48 hr but not at log phase (Figure 1F), and also under-expressed in set1H1017L and spp1Δ mutants (data not shown), suggesting that cryptic functions for H3K4 methylation in facilitating gene expression are unmasked during the widespread gene induction that accompanies ageing.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K4 methylation-dependent expression defects appear specifically during aging.

claim: 107 genes were significantly different between wild type and COMPASS mutants at log phase.
source: 107 genes were significantly different between wild type and COMPASS mutants at log phase, with more being differentially expressed at 24 and 48 hr (389 and 488), but few at 7.5 hr (39).
evidence: Supported by DESeq2 differential expression analysis.

claim: 389 genes were significantly different between wild type and COMPASS mutants at 24 hr.
source: 107 genes were significantly different between wild type and COMPASS mutants at log phase, with more being differentially expressed at 24 and 48 hr (389 and 488), but few at 7.5 hr (39).
evidence: Supported by DESeq2 differential expression analysis.

claim: 488 genes were significantly different between wild type and COMPASS mutants at 48 hr.
source: 107 genes were significantly different between wild type and COMPASS mutants at log phase, with more being differentially expressed at 24 and 48 hr (389 and 488), but few at 7.5 hr (39).
evidence: Supported by DESeq2 differential expression analysis.

claim: Log phase cells contain a subset of genes that are substantially over-expressed in COMPASS mutants (on average 3-fold), but this difference disappears with age.
source: Interestingly, log phase cells contain a subset of genes that are substantially over-expressed in COMPASS mutants (on average 3-fold), but this difference disappears with age (Figure 2A, top).
evidence: Supported by differential expression data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Significantly under-expressed genes at log phase are on average only less than 1.5 fold lower than in wild type.
source: In contrast, significantly under-expressed genes at log phase are on average only <1.5 fold lower than in wild type, but with age many more genes become under-expressed in COMPASS mutants and to a greater degree (2-fold on average, but many are 3 – 4-fold reduced) (Figure 2A, bottom), suggesting that the role of COMPASS in gene expression is age dependent.
evidence: Supported by differential expression data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: With age many more genes become under-expressed in COMPASS mutants and to a greater degree (2-fold on average, but many are 3-4-fold reduced).
source: In contrast, significantly under-expressed genes at log phase are on average only <1.5 fold lower than in wild type, but with age many more genes become under-expressed in COMPASS mutants and to a greater degree (2-fold on average, but many are 3 – 4-fold reduced) (Figure 2A, bottom), suggesting that the role of COMPASS in gene expression is age dependent.
evidence: Supported by differential expression data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The role of COMPASS in gene expression is age dependent.
source: In contrast, significantly under-expressed genes at log phase are on average only <1.5 fold lower than in wild type, but with age many more genes become under-expressed in COMPASS mutants and to a greater degree (2-fold on average, but many are 3 – 4-fold reduced) (Figure 2A, bottom), suggesting that the role of COMPASS in gene expression is age dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the magnitude and number of expression defects increase with age.

claim: Over-expressed genes at 48 hr (191) were primarily enriched for ribosome-related terms.
source: Starting with the 48 hr time point, we segregated under- and over-expressed genes and performed GO analyses (Figure 2B and Table S1). Over-expressed genes (191) were primarily enriched for ribosome-related terms as expected (Weiner et al., 2012), but under-expressed genes (297) were enriched for cell wall organisation and de novo NAD+ biosynthesis, both of which are known to be important for maintenance of replicative lifespan (Bonkowski and Sinclair, 2016; Molon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2B and citation.

claim: Under-expressed genes at 48 hr (297) were enriched for cell wall organisation and de novo NAD+ biosynthesis.
source: Starting with the 48 hr time point, we segregated under- and over-expressed genes and performed GO analyses (Figure 2B and Table S1). Over-expressed genes (191) were primarily enriched for ribosome-related terms as expected (Weiner et al., 2012), but under-expressed genes (297) were enriched for cell wall organisation and de novo NAD+ biosynthesis, both of which are known to be important for maintenance of replicative lifespan (Bonkowski and Sinclair, 2016; Molon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2B and citations.

claim: Cell wall organisation and de novo NAD+ biosynthesis are known to be important for maintenance of replicative lifespan.
source: Starting with the 48 hr time point, we segregated under- and over-expressed genes and performed GO analyses (Figure 2B and Table S1). Over-expressed genes (191) were primarily enriched for ribosome-related terms as expected (Weiner et al., 2012), but under-expressed genes (297) were enriched for cell wall organisation and de novo NAD+ biosynthesis, both of which are known to be important for maintenance of replicative lifespan (Bonkowski and Sinclair, 2016; Molon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on lifespan determinants.

claim: All COMPASS mutations had a similar effect on expression.
source: Although these genes were identified using a pooled dataset from three COMPASS mutants, all the COMPASS mutations had a similar effect on expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An equivalent analysis comparing wild type to swd1Δ identified 240 under-expressed genes at 48 hr of which 60% overlapped with those identified in the pooled COMPASS mutant dataset.
source: Furthermore, an equivalent analysis comparing wild type to swd1Δ identified 240 under-expressed genes at 48 hr of which 60% overlapped with those identified in the pooled COMPASS mutant dataset (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Table S1), and GO analysis of these 240 genes also indicated effects on cell wall biosynthesis and nicotinamide metabolism.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In comparisons of wild-type to pooled COMPASS mutants or swd1Δ, the majority of genes affected by loss of COMPASS failed to be properly upregulated with age.
source: Notably, in comparisons of wild-type to pooled COMPASS mutants or swd1Δ, the majority of genes affected by loss of COMPASS failed to be properly upregulated with age; this behaviour has not been observed in other transitions – Margaritis et al. examined the massive transcriptional reprogramming that accompanies the transition from stationary phase to log phase growth and found 220 genes mis-regulated of which only 24 (10%) were under-expressed in COMPASS mutants (Margaritis et al., 2012), compared to 297 (61%) of significantly altered genes that we observe in aged cells.
evidence: Supported by comparison to previous study and current data.

claim: 104 genes were significantly under-expressed in aged spp1Δ cells compared to wild type along with 19 over-expressed genes.
source: We employed a more relaxed significance threshold (p<0.05) for differential expression analysis to reflect the fact that spp1Δ is not a complete loss-of-function mutant as some residual H3K4me3 is still present (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and is therefore expected to cause a weaker phenotype; this yielded 104 significantly under-expressed genes in aged spp1Δ cells compared to wild type along with 19 over-expressed genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GO analysis of the under-expressed genes in spp1Δ revealed significant enrichments for cell wall biogenesis and de novo NAD+ biosynthesis.
source: GO analysis of the under-expressed genes again revealed significant enrichments for cell wall biogenesis and de novo NAD+ biosynthesis just as in the combined COMPASS mutant set, showing that proper expression of these genes is dependent on H3K4me3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Proper expression of cell wall biogenesis and de novo NAD+ biosynthesis genes is dependent on H3K4me3.
source: GO analysis of the under-expressed genes again revealed significant enrichments for cell wall biogenesis and de novo NAD+ biosynthesis just as in the combined COMPASS mutant set, showing that proper expression of these genes is dependent on H3K4me3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that spp1Δ, which specifically affects H3K4me3, shows similar GO enrichments.

claim: H3K4me2 levels were similar in both wild-type and spp1Δ strains in young and old cells.
source: To confirm that COMPASS activity is globally similar in young and old cells we probed western blots of log phase and 24 hour-aged wild-type and spp1Δ cells for H3K4me2 and H3K4me3. This confirmed that H3K4me2 levels were similar in both strains in young and old cells, and that Spp1 is also required for H3K4me3 in old cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Spp1 is required for H3K4me3 in old cells.
source: To confirm that COMPASS activity is globally similar in young and old cells we probed western blots of log phase and 24 hour-aged wild-type and spp1Δ cells for H3K4me2 and H3K4me3. This confirmed that H3K4me2 levels were similar in both strains in young and old cells, and that Spp1 is also required for H3K4me3 in old cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Approximately 4.5% of genes require COMPASS to attain normal expression over the period of the yeast replicative lifespan.
source: Overall, although COMPASS mutants are considered to have little impact on gene expression in log phase, we detect many genes (~4.5%) that require COMPASS to attain normal expression over the period of the yeast replicative lifespan.
evidence: Calculated from the number of differentially expressed genes relative to total genes.

claim: BNA1, BNA2 and BNA4-7 encode the enzymes required for biosynthesis of the NAD+-precursor NaMN from tryptophan.
source: BNA1, BNA2 and BNA4-7 encode the enzymes required for biosynthesis of the NAD+-precursor NaMN from tryptophan (Figure 3A), and differential expression of these genes underlies the GO enrichment for de novo biosynthesis of NAD+ in ageing COMPASS mutants described in the previous section.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of NAD+ biosynthesis pathway and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: BNA1, BNA2, BNA4, BNA5 and BNA6 are all induced with age and this induction is impaired in spp1Δ.
source: We first assessed the expression of these genes individually across age in the RNAseq dataset. BNA1, BNA2, BNA4, BNA5 and BNA6 are all induced with age and this induction is impaired in spp1Δ, with BNA7 forming an outlier that is unchanged by age or SPP1 deletion (Figure 3B compare wild type to spp1Δ).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: BNA7 is unchanged by age or SPP1 deletion.
source: We first assessed the expression of these genes individually across age in the RNAseq dataset. BNA1, BNA2, BNA4, BNA5 and BNA6 are all induced with age and this induction is impaired in spp1Δ, with BNA7 forming an outlier that is unchanged by age or SPP1 deletion (Figure 3B compare wild type to spp1Δ).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The induced gene expression level of BNA1, BNA4 and BNA5 was significantly reduced in spp1Δ cells.
source: The induced gene expression level of BNA1, BNA4 and BNA5 was significantly reduced in spp1Δ cells, with BNA6 showing a similar trend (Figure 3C,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3C,D and supplements.

claim: BNA1, BNA5 and BNA6 were significantly under-expressed in spp1Δ even in the absence of nicotinamide treatment.
source: Furthermore BNA1, BNA5 and BNA6 were significantly under-expressed even in the absence of nicotinamide treatment.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data comparing untreated conditions.

claim: BNA7 was not induced by nicotinamide and was unaffected in spp1Δ cells.
source: In contrast, BNA7 was not induced by nicotinamide and was unaffected in spp1Δ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The impact of H3K4me3 on BNA gene expression is not restricted to ageing cells.
source: These results matched the RNAseq data for log and 48hr-aged cells remarkably well (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B,C compare left and right panels), showing that the impact of H3K4me3 is not restricted to ageing cells and therefore that H3K4me3 is required to maintain both basal and induced expression levels of the BNA genes.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity between nicotinamide induction in log phase cells and age-linked induction.

claim: H3K4me3 is required to maintain both basal and induced expression levels of the BNA genes.
source: These results matched the RNAseq data for log and 48hr-aged cells remarkably well (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B,C compare left and right panels), showing that the impact of H3K4me3 is not restricted to ageing cells and therefore that H3K4me3 is required to maintain both basal and induced expression levels of the BNA genes.
evidence: Supported by comparison of basal and induced expression in spp1Δ mutants.

claim: H3K4 mutant phenotypes for BNA4-7 are very similar to swd1Δ.
source: As before we used nicotinamide to induce expression of the BNA genes in haploid cells growing at log phase in YPD, and observed that the H3K4 mutants largely phenocopied the COMPASS mutants; H3K4 mutant phenotypes for BNA4-7 are very similar to swd1Δ, while the phenotype for BNA1 lies in-between that of swd1Δ and spp1Δ (Figure 3E,F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3E,F and supplements.

claim: The phenotype for BNA1 in H3K4 mutants lies in-between that of swd1Δ and spp1Δ.
source: As before we used nicotinamide to induce expression of the BNA genes in haploid cells growing at log phase in YPD, and observed that the H3K4 mutants largely phenocopied the COMPASS mutants; H3K4 mutant phenotypes for BNA4-7 are very similar to swd1Δ, while the phenotype for BNA1 lies in-between that of swd1Δ and spp1Δ (Figure 3E,F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3E,F and supplements.

claim: COMPASS acts through H3K4 methylation to alter the expression of the BNA genes.
source: This is consistent with COMPASS acting through H3K4 methylation to alter the expression of the BNA genes.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between COMPASS mutants and H3K4 mutants.

claim: COMPASS mutation affects the expression of NAD+ biosynthesis genes directly via H3K4 methylation, rather than through indirect age-induced changes in metabolism.
source: Together, these data show that COMPASS mutation affects the expression of NAD+ biosynthesis genes directly via H3K4 methylation, rather than through indirect age-induced changes in metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that effects are seen in young cells treated with nicotinamide.

claim: There is a critical role of H3K4me3 in maintaining the normal expression of yeast genes.
source: They further provide strong evidence for a critical role of H3K4me3 in maintaining the normal expression of yeast genes.
evidence: Inferred from the consistent under-expression of BNA genes in spp1Δ mutants.

claim: With age, the signal from promoter associated H3K4me3 peaks increased and the spread of H3K4me3 signals was compressed.
source: With age, the signal from promoter associated H3K4me3 peaks increased and the spread of H3K4me3 signals was compressed (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a progressive loss of repressed promoters with no detectable H3K4me3 peak with age.
source: Particularly notable is the progressive loss of repressed promoters with no detectable H3K4me3 peak (Figure 4A grey arrows).
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between age-linked gene induction and change in promoter H3K4me3 signal.
source: These observations are consistent with H3K4me3 peaks at inactive or low activity promoters becoming more prominent as would be expected from the genome-wide induction of low-expressed genes, and indeed we observe a strong positive correlation between age-linked gene induction and change in promoter H3K4me3 signal (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: By 48 hr, the promoter H3K4me3 peak became less defined, due to increasing H3K4me3 in gene bodies and intergenic regions.
source: By 48 hr, the promoter H3K4me3 peak also became less defined, due to increasing H3K4me3 in gene bodies and intergenic regions (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq profile shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For the 300 least induced genes, which are highly expressed throughout life, there is on average a reduction of the H3K4me3 peak between 24 and 48 hr.
source: This behaviour is somewhat variable across genes: for the 300 least induced genes, which are highly expressed throughout life, we observe on average a reduction of the H3K4me3 peak between 24 and 48 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), but in contrast the 300 most induced genes, which have very low log phase expression, show a dramatic age-linked increase in H3K4me3 in the region round the TSS as well as the appearance of a small H3K4me3 peak (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq profile shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The 300 most induced genes, which have very low log phase expression, show a dramatic age-linked increase in H3K4me3 in the region round the TSS as well as the appearance of a small H3K4me3 peak.
source: This behaviour is somewhat variable across genes: for the 300 least induced genes, which are highly expressed throughout life, we observe on average a reduction of the H3K4me3 peak between 24 and 48 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), but in contrast the 300 most induced genes, which have very low log phase expression, show a dramatic age-linked increase in H3K4me3 in the region round the TSS as well as the appearance of a small H3K4me3 peak (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq profile shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Antisense transcripts increase substantially with age and to a similar extent for all genes.
source: To assess this, we quantified antisense poly(A)+RNA for annotated genes and found that antisense transcripts increase substantially with age and to a similar extent for all genes, despite clear differences in age-linked expression change for the sense mRNA (compare Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by antisense RNA analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Upregulation of antisense transcription independent of sense transcript expression is indicative of a genome-wide increase in pervasive transcription.
source: This upregulation of antisense transcription independent of sense transcript expression is indicative of a genome-wide increase in pervasive transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that antisense transcription increases uniformly across genes.

claim: Age-linked changes in promoter-associated H3K4me3 are consistent with genome-wide gene induction.
source: Overall, age-linked changes in promoter-associated H3K4me3 are consistent with genome-wide gene induction, but the tight promoter association of H3K4me3 is compromised in old cells and H3K4me3 accumulates in non-promoter regions in accord with an observed increase in pervasive transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between H3K4me3 changes and gene expression changes.

claim: The tight promoter association of H3K4me3 is compromised in old cells.
source: Overall, age-linked changes in promoter-associated H3K4me3 are consistent with genome-wide gene induction, but the tight promoter association of H3K4me3 is compromised in old cells and H3K4me3 accumulates in non-promoter regions in accord with an observed increase in pervasive transcription.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data showing spreading of H3K4me3 signal.

claim: There is a 7-fold rDNA copy number increase from log to 48 hr based on ChIP input material.
source: The rDNA was analysed separately as this region is massively amplified during ageing; we observe a 7-fold rDNA copy number increase from log to 48 hr based on ChIP input material (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), consistent with known accumulation of extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs) and other extrachromosomal rDNA species (Pal et al., 2018; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: Supported by input DNA analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and citations.

claim: Non-rDNA regions gain H3K4me3 between log and 48 hr of age.
source: Non-rDNA regions gain H3K4me3 between log and 48 hr of age as noted above, while rDNA H3K4me3 shows a striking rise from very low levels at log phase to the same level as non-rDNA regions by 48 hr consistent with a complete loss of rDNA silencing (Figure 4E) (Li et al., 2017; Pal et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by H3K4me3 density analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: rDNA H3K4me3 shows a striking rise from very low levels at log phase to the same level as non-rDNA regions by 48 hr consistent with a complete loss of rDNA silencing.
source: Non-rDNA regions gain H3K4me3 between log and 48 hr of age as noted above, while rDNA H3K4me3 shows a striking rise from very low levels at log phase to the same level as non-rDNA regions by 48 hr consistent with a complete loss of rDNA silencing (Figure 4E) (Li et al., 2017; Pal et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by H3K4me3 density analysis shown in Figure 4E and citations.

claim: The total amount of H3K4me3 in the genome increases 2-fold by 48 hr.
source: However, the massive increase in rDNA copy number results in unexpected changes in global distributions of both H3K4me3 and H3: the combination of loss of rDNA silencing with increased copy number leads to the total amount of H3K4me3 in the genome increasing 2-fold by 48 hr, with the proportion of H3K4me3 in rDNA rising from 2.5% to 40% (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by summed H3K4me3 signal analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The proportion of H3K4me3 in rDNA rises from 2.5% to 40% by 48 hr.
source: However, the massive increase in rDNA copy number results in unexpected changes in global distributions of both H3K4me3 and H3: the combination of loss of rDNA silencing with increased copy number leads to the total amount of H3K4me3 in the genome increasing 2-fold by 48 hr, with the proportion of H3K4me3 in rDNA rising from 2.5% to 40% (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by summed H3K4me3 signal analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There is a small (approximately 1.3 fold) increase in H3, driven by increases in rDNA copy number.
source: This is accompanied by a small (~1.3 fold) increase in H3, again driven by increases in rDNA copy number (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by summed H3 signal analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The amount of H3K4me3 in the cell rises with age relative to H3.
source: Taken together, these results implied that the amount of H3K4me3 in the cell should rise with age relative to H3, an effect that we confirmed independently by western blot (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Age-associated genome-wide gene induction is accompanied by rising promoter H3K4me3.
source: These data show that age-associated genome-wide gene induction is accompanied by rising promoter H3K4me3, and that H3K4me3 accumulates both in non-promoter regions and in the rDNA as cells age, associated with loss of rDNA heterochromatin and increased genome-wide pervasive transcription.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq and RNAseq data showing coordinated changes.

claim: H3K4me3 accumulates both in non-promoter regions and in the rDNA as cells age, associated with loss of rDNA heterochromatin and increased genome-wide pervasive transcription.
source: These data show that age-associated genome-wide gene induction is accompanied by rising promoter H3K4me3, and that H3K4me3 accumulates both in non-promoter regions and in the rDNA as cells age, associated with loss of rDNA heterochromatin and increased genome-wide pervasive transcription.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data showing H3K4me3 distribution changes and antisense transcription data.

claim: A large subset of yeast genes depend on H3K4me3 to attain normal expression levels.
source: Here, we have shown that a large subset of yeast genes depend on H3K4me3 to attain normal expression levels.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis showing hundreds of genes under-expressed in COMPASS mutants.

claim: This effect of H3K4me3 on gene expression becomes prevalent during the ageing process in which huge numbers of genes are induced coincident with a decline in the repressive capacity of H3K4 methylation.
source: This effect becomes prevalent during the ageing process in which huge numbers of genes are induced coincident with a decline in the repressive capacity of H3K4 methylation.
evidence: Supported by age-dependent changes in gene expression defects in COMPASS mutants.

claim: H3K4me3 is an epigenetic mark that facilitates gene expression.
source: Our results provide a clear demonstration that H3K4me3 is indeed an epigenetic mark that facilitates gene expression, and one that plays a critical role in maintaining cell viability across the life-course.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing H3K4me3-dependent gene expression and lifespan effects.

claim: H3K4me3 plays a critical role in maintaining cell viability across the life-course.
source: Our results provide a clear demonstration that H3K4me3 is indeed an epigenetic mark that facilitates gene expression, and one that plays a critical role in maintaining cell viability across the life-course.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data showing reduced viability in H3K4me3-defective mutants.

claim: H3K4 methylation has a remarkably complex effect on gene expression.
source: H3K4 methylation has a remarkably complex effect on gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of both repressive and activating effects.

claim: Transcriptomic approaches have detected repressive functions of H3K4 methylation.
source: Transcriptomic approaches have detected repressive functions (Guillemette et al., 2011; Jaiswal et al., 2017; Lenstra et al., 2011; Margaritis et al., 2012; Venkatasubrahmanyam et al., 2007), although in most cases this can probably be attributed to H3K4me2 with the possible exception of ribosomal protein genes (Weiner et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to transcriptomic studies.

claim: Repressive functions of H3K4 methylation can probably be attributed to H3K4me2 with the possible exception of ribosomal protein genes.
source: Transcriptomic approaches have detected repressive functions (Guillemette et al., 2011; Jaiswal et al., 2017; Lenstra et al., 2011; Margaritis et al., 2012; Venkatasubrahmanyam et al., 2007), although in most cases this can probably be attributed to H3K4me2 with the possible exception of ribosomal protein genes (Weiner et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of mutants affecting different methylation states and citation.

claim: If H3K4 methylation has both repressive and inducing activities, the outcome of COMPASS mutations on individual genes would be expected to vary by gene, by genetic background and by experimental system.
source: Setting aside technical issues, if H3K4 methylation has both repressive and inducing activities, the outcome of COMPASS mutations on individual genes would be expected to vary by gene, by genetic background and by experimental system, making broad conclusions rather treacherous.
evidence: Logical inference from the premise of dual activities.

claim: Antagonism between activating and repressive activities would help explain the conflicting data in the literature.
source: Antagonism between activating and repressive activities would help explain the conflicting data in the literature, and close examination of the data in Figure 3 provides support for this: loss of Spp1 reduces expression for most of the BNA genes, whereas loss of Swd1 has a milder and more variable effect that likely results from the summed outcomes of repressive H3K4me2 and activating H3K4me3 (see summary of H3K4me3 and H3K4me2 effects on the BNA genes in Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of spp1Δ and swd1Δ phenotypes and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Loss of Spp1 reduces expression for most of the BNA genes.
source: Antagonism between activating and repressive activities would help explain the conflicting data in the literature, and close examination of the data in Figure 3 provides support for this: loss of Spp1 reduces expression for most of the BNA genes, whereas loss of Swd1 has a milder and more variable effect that likely results from the summed outcomes of repressive H3K4me2 and activating H3K4me3 (see summary of H3K4me3 and H3K4me2 effects on the BNA genes in Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data in Figure 3.

claim: Loss of Swd1 has a milder and more variable effect on BNA gene expression that likely results from the summed outcomes of repressive H3K4me2 and activating H3K4me3.
source: Antagonism between activating and repressive activities would help explain the conflicting data in the literature, and close examination of the data in Figure 3 provides support for this: loss of Spp1 reduces expression for most of the BNA genes, whereas loss of Swd1 has a milder and more variable effect that likely results from the summed outcomes of repressive H3K4me2 and activating H3K4me3 (see summary of H3K4me3 and H3K4me2 effects on the BNA genes in Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of swd1Δ and spp1Δ phenotypes and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: At BNA7, H3K4me2 appears to be activating while H3K4me3 has no effect.
source: However for other genes, the balance and direction of these effects is clearly different, for example at BNA7 H3K4me2 appears to be activating while H3K4me3 has no effect.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BNA7 is reduced in swd1Δ but not spp1Δ.

claim: The impact of H3K4 methylation cannot be generalised but must be considered on a gene-by-gene basis taking into account both repressive and activating effects.
source: Therefore, the impact of H3K4 methylation cannot be generalised but must be considered on a gene-by-gene basis taking into account both repressive and activating effects.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of variable effects across different genes.

claim: Binding of Yng1, Yng2 or Sgf29 would recruit NuA3, NuA4 or SAGA histone acetyl transferase complexes respectively, promoting local histone acetylation that should enhance transcriptional activation.
source: Binding of Yng1, Yng2 or Sgf29 would recruit NuA3, NuA4 or SAGA histone acetyl transferase complexes respectively, promoting local histone acetylation that should enhance transcriptional activation (Agalioti et al., 2002; Bian et al., 2011; Pokholok et al., 2005; Steunou et al., 2016; Taverna et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on H3K4me3-binding proteins and their functions.

claim: Loss of recruitment of NuA3 and NuA4 to H3K4me3 has remarkably little effect on gene expression under normal conditions.
source: Loss of recruitment of NuA3 and NuA4 to H3K4me3 has remarkably little effect on gene expression under normal conditions (Choy et al., 2001; Taverna et al., 2006), but may well impact a specific subset of genes when induced during environmental change or during dramatic chromatin remodelling of the sort that occurs during ageing; indeed delays in induction of individual genes have been reported in mutants lacking H3K4me3-linked acetyltransferase recruitment (Bian et al., 2011; Morillon et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on NuA3 and NuA4 function.

claim: H3K4 methylation and in particular H3K4me3 is critical for the maintenance of a normal lifespan.
source: Our experiments very clearly show that H3K4 methylation and in particular H3K4me3 is critical for the maintenance of a normal lifespan.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data showing reduced viability in COMPASS mutants.

claim: 43% of yeast genes are differentially expressed during ageing.
source: We observed 43% of yeast genes to be differentially expressed during ageing, of which 17% show significantly different expression levels in COMPASS mutants after 48 hr.
evidence: Calculated from differential expression analysis.

claim: 17% of genes differentially expressed during ageing show significantly different expression levels in COMPASS mutants after 48 hr.
source: We observed 43% of yeast genes to be differentially expressed during ageing, of which 17% show significantly different expression levels in COMPASS mutants after 48 hr.
evidence: Calculated from differential expression analysis.

claim: As cells age, loss of H3K4 methylation has a dramatic effect on maintenance of normal gene expression patterns.
source: This means that as cells age, loss of H3K4 methylation has a dramatic effect on maintenance of normal gene expression patterns.
evidence: Inferred from the large number of genes mis-expressed in COMPASS mutants during aging.

claim: There is a progressive loss of the repressive capacity of H3K4 methylation as cells age.
source: We observed a progressive loss of the repressive capacity of H3K4 methylation as cells age, however this is probably not the cause of the lifespan defect, as the repressive activity is not impacted by spp1Δ whereas lifespan is similar in swd1Δ and spp1Δ cells.
evidence: Supported by differential expression data showing reduced over-expression in COMPASS mutants with age.

claim: The loss of repressive capacity of H3K4 methylation is probably not the cause of the lifespan defect in COMPASS mutants.
source: We observed a progressive loss of the repressive capacity of H3K4 methylation as cells age, however this is probably not the cause of the lifespan defect, as the repressive activity is not impacted by spp1Δ whereas lifespan is similar in swd1Δ and spp1Δ cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that spp1Δ has similar lifespan defect but does not show repressive defects.

claim: The most prominent gene expression effect in COMPASS mutants was a failure to fully induce hundreds of genes.
source: Rather, the most prominent gene expression effect was a failure to fully induce hundreds of genes in COMPASS mutants including spp1Δ.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis showing under-expression of many genes.

claim: NAD+ biosynthesis genes are unlikely to explain the shortened lifespan of COMPASS mutants alone.
source: We validated this role of COMPASS for expression of NAD+ biosynthesis genes, but these constitute only a handful of the significantly mis-expressed genes and are unlikely to explain the shortened lifespan of COMPASS mutants alone.
evidence: Inferred from the small number of NAD+ biosynthesis genes relative to total mis-expressed genes.

claim: Given the widespread age-linked gene mis-regulation in COMPASS mutants, it is not surprising that the lifespan of these cells is profoundly reduced.
source: In reality, given the widespread age-linked gene mis-regulation in COMPASS mutants, it is not surprising that the lifespan of these cells is profoundly reduced.
evidence: Inferred from the large number of mis-expressed genes and observed lifespan defects.

claim: H3K4me3 is progressively gained at euchromatic promoters in accord with genome-wide gene induction, despite a mild reduction in H3 density.
source: ChIP experiments show that H3K4me3 is progressively gained at euchromatic promoters in accord with genome-wide gene induction, despite a mild reduction in H3 density.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data showing H3K4me3 and H3 changes.

claim: Spike-in normalisation was critical for obtaining accurate measurements of H3K4me3 as normalisation to internal standards erroneously shows loss of H3K4me3 with age.
source: Spike-in normalisation was critical for obtaining accurate measurements of H3K4me3 as normalisation to internal standards erroneously shows loss of H3K4me3 with age, emphasising the importance of normalisation controls in ageing studies (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of spike-in normalized and non-normalized data, supported by citation.

claim: The increase in H3K4me3 across euchromatic promoters is dwarfed by the massive accumulation of H3K4me3 in rDNA, resulting in greater than 2 fold increase in H3K4me3 across the genome.
source: The increase in H3K4me3 across euchromatic promoters is however dwarfed by the massive accumulation of H3K4me3 in rDNA, resulting in >2 fold increase in H3K4me3 across the genome.
evidence: Supported by summed H3K4me3 signal analysis.

claim: H3K4me3 is involved in recruitment of pro-expression factors.
source: As noted above, H3K4me3 is involved in recruitment of pro-expression factors, but repressors such as the Set3 and Rpd3 complexes are recruited to H3K4me2 (Kim and Buratowski, 2009; Pinskaya et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on H3K4me3-binding proteins.

claim: Repressors such as the Set3 and Rpd3 complexes are recruited to H3K4me2.
source: As noted above, H3K4me3 is involved in recruitment of pro-expression factors, but repressors such as the Set3 and Rpd3 complexes are recruited to H3K4me2 (Kim and Buratowski, 2009; Pinskaya et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on H3K4me2-binding proteins.

claim: Accumulation of H3K4me2 in amplified rDNA would titrate repressive factors.
source: It is largely this age-linked loss of repressive activity that allowed us to detect pro-expression activities of H3K4me3, and it is tempting to speculate that accumulation of H3K4me2 in amplified rDNA (which is strongly predicted based on our data) would titrate repressive factors.
evidence: Speculative inference based on rDNA amplification and H3K4me2 function.

claim: The density of H3 in euchromatin decreases in aged samples.
source: Similarly, although the density of H3 in euchromatin decreases in aged samples in our experiments as previously reported (Hu et al., 2014), we find that this is more than offset by the increase in H3 associated with rDNA.
evidence: Supported by H3 ChIPseq data and citation.

claim: The decrease in H3 density in euchromatin is more than offset by the increase in H3 associated with rDNA.
source: Similarly, although the density of H3 in euchromatin decreases in aged samples in our experiments as previously reported (Hu et al., 2014), we find that this is more than offset by the increase in H3 associated with rDNA.
evidence: Supported by summed H3 signal analysis.

claim: Cells struggle to maintain histone supply in the face of the almost doubling of genome size caused by profligate rDNA amplification.
source: It is not hard to imagine that cells struggle to maintain histone supply in the face of the almost doubling of genome size caused by profligate rDNA amplification; although different groups have reported either decreased or unchanging histone supply with age (Feser et al., 2010; Janssens et al., 2015), there is no indication that supply increases to match demand caused by rDNA amplification.
evidence: Inferred from genome size increase and citations on histone supply.

claim: One result of rDNA amplification through ERC accumulation is to titrate histones and histone binding factors.
source: It seems very likely to us that one result of rDNA amplification through ERC accumulation is to titrate histones and histone binding factors, and this will provide an important focus for future studies into age-linked gene expression change.
evidence: Speculative inference based on rDNA amplification and histone/factor availability.

claim: Promoter recruitment of COMPASS starts with the RNA pol II elongation factors Paf and FACT, which activate the H2B-ubiquitylation activity of Rad6/Bre1.
source: Promoter recruitment of COMPASS starts with the RNA pol II elongation factors Paf and FACT, which activate the H2B-ubiquitylation activity of Rad6/Bre1 (Pavri et al., 2006); this activity, and a non-mutated H2B123K substrate, are vital for COMPASS recruitment and di-/tri-methylation (Dover et al., 2002; Krogan et al., 2003; Sun and Allis, 2002; Wood et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on COMPASS recruitment mechanism.

claim: H2B-ubiquitylation activity and a non-mutated H2B123K substrate are vital for COMPASS recruitment and di-/tri-methylation.
source: Promoter recruitment of COMPASS starts with the RNA pol II elongation factors Paf and FACT, which activate the H2B-ubiquitylation activity of Rad6/Bre1 (Pavri et al., 2006); this activity, and a non-mutated H2B123K substrate, are vital for COMPASS recruitment and di-/tri-methylation (Dover et al., 2002; Krogan et al., 2003; Sun and Allis, 2002; Wood et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on COMPASS recruitment mechanism.

claim: Activation of Rad6/Bre1 and COMPASS recruitment require interactions with the Ser-5 phosphorylated CTD of RNA polymerase II.
source: Activation of Rad6/Bre1 and COMPASS recruitment also require interactions with the Ser-5 phosphorylated CTD of RNA polymerase II, providing a tight transcriptional connection (Krogan et al., 2003; Ng et al., 2003; Xiao et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on COMPASS recruitment mechanism.

claim: COMPASS recruitment occurs through interactions of Swd2 with active H2B-associated Rad6/Bre1, and of Set1/Spp1 with nascent mRNA.
source: COMPASS recruitment then occurs through interactions of Swd2 with active H2B-associated Rad6/Bre1, and of Set1/Spp1 with nascent mRNA (Battaglia et al., 2017; Luciano et al., 2017; Sayou et al., 2017; Thornton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on COMPASS recruitment mechanism.

claim: In mammals, additional CxxC domains in Cfp1 and some SET-domain proteins allow DNA methylation-dependent activity and selective recruitment of COMPASS to promoter and enhancer sequences.
source: In mammals, additional CxxC domains in Cfp1 (the orthologue of yeast Spp1) and some SET-domain proteins further specify and diversify COMPASS activity, allowing DNA methylation-dependent activity and selective recruitment of COMPASS to promoter and enhancer sequences (Brown et al., 2017; Clouaire et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2017; Thomson et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mammalian COMPASS.

claim: Loss of Set1 does not drastically impair transcription in yeast.
source: The importance of H3K4me3 in transcription has been difficult to study as loss of Set1 also abrogates H3K4me1 and H3K4me2. Even so, loss of Set1 does not drastically impair transcription in yeast, and the extent to which subsets of genes are mis-regulated in set1Δ cells has been controversial with later studies reporting mostly gene upregulation (Guillemette et al., 2011; Margaritis et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2001; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002; Venkatasubrahmanyam et al., 2007; Weiner et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on set1Δ phenotypes.

claim: Later studies report mostly gene upregulation in set1Δ cells.
source: The importance of H3K4me3 in transcription has been difficult to study as loss of Set1 also abrogates H3K4me1 and H3K4me2. Even so, loss of Set1 does not drastically impair transcription in yeast, and the extent to which subsets of genes are mis-regulated in set1Δ cells has been controversial with later studies reporting mostly gene upregulation (Guillemette et al., 2011; Margaritis et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2001; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002; Venkatasubrahmanyam et al., 2007; Weiner et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to transcriptomic studies.

claim: H3K4 methylation has a primarily repressive role, particularly evident for ribosome synthesis factors, non-coding RNA-regulated genes and heterochromatic regions.
source: This suggests a primarily repressive role for H3K4 methylation, particularly evident for ribosome synthesis factors (Weiner et al., 2012), non-coding RNA-regulated genes (Berretta et al., 2008; Camblong et al., 2009; Pinskaya et al., 2009) and heterochromatic regions (Briggs et al., 2001; Li et al., 2006; Nislow et al., 1997; Venkatasubrahmanyam et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on H3K4 methylation function.

claim: Studies in yeast focusing on cells lacking Spp1 have observed virtually no impact on steady state gene expression or on acute gene induction during media shifts.
source: To determine the importance of H3K4me3 specifically, studies in yeast have focused on cells lacking Spp1 which is required for most (but not all) H3K4me3, and have observed virtually no impact on steady state gene expression or on acute gene induction during media shifts (Howe et al., 2017; Margaritis et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on spp1Δ phenotypes.

claim: Loss of CFP1 in mammalian cells has concrete effects on gene expression, causing both up- and down-regulation of many genes in mouse ES cells and reduced transcription in oocytes.
source: In contrast, loss of CFP1 in mammalian cells has concrete effects on gene expression, causing both up- and down-regulation of many genes in mouse ES cells and reduced transcription in oocytes (Brown et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on CFP1 function in mammals.

claim: H3K4me3 is mechanistically tied to activation of p53-regulated genes in response to DNA damage through recruitment of TAF3 in HCT116 cells.
source: One specific report ties H3K4me3 mechanistically to activation of p53-regulated genes in response to DNA damage through recruitment of TAF3 in HCT116 cells, however this may be cell-type specific as the same response was not impaired in mouse ES cells lacking CFP1 (Clouaire et al., 2014; Lauberth et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on H3K4me3 function in DNA damage response.

claim: H3K4 methylation has the potential to both repress and activate transcription.
source: Overall, H3K4 methylation has the potential to both repress and activate transcription, but a general role for H3K4me3 in transcriptional activation remains unproven.
evidence: Inferred from the diverse effects observed in different studies.

claim: A general role for H3K4me3 in transcriptional activation remains unproven.
source: Overall, H3K4 methylation has the potential to both repress and activate transcription, but a general role for H3K4me3 in transcriptional activation remains unproven.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of consistent evidence across studies.

claim: An association between histone modifications and ageing is well recognised.
source: An association between histone modifications and ageing is well recognised (reviewed in [Maleszewska et al., 2016]).
evidence: Supported by citation to review.

claim: Defects in H3K4, H3K36 and H3K27 methylation all affect lifespan presumably through impacts on gene expression.
source: For example, defects in H3K4, H3K36 and H3K27 methylation all affect lifespan presumably through impacts on gene expression, though in most cases the downstream expression differences remain obscure (Alvares et al., 2014; Greer et al., 2010; Li et al., 2010; Maures et al., 2011; McColl et al., 2008; Sen et al., 2015; Siebold et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on histone methylation and lifespan.

claim: A gross genome-wide loss of histones has been reported to accompany ageing in yeast and cultured human cells.
source: Remarkably, a gross genome-wide loss of histones has been reported to accompany ageing in yeast and cultured human cells (Feser et al., 2010; Ivanov et al., 2013; O'Sullivan et al., 2010), leading to an opening of chromatin structure particularly at repressed promoters and causing widespread induction of normally repressed genes (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on histone loss during aging.

claim: Histone loss leads to an opening of chromatin structure particularly at repressed promoters and causes widespread induction of normally repressed genes.
source: Remarkably, a gross genome-wide loss of histones has been reported to accompany ageing in yeast and cultured human cells (Feser et al., 2010; Ivanov et al., 2013; O'Sullivan et al., 2010), leading to an opening of chromatin structure particularly at repressed promoters and causing widespread induction of normally repressed genes (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on chromatin structure changes during aging.

claim: General opening of chromatin structure has been proposed to underlie many age-linked gene expression differences.
source: General opening of chromatin structure has therefore been proposed to underlie many age-linked gene expression differences (Hu et al., 2014), and it is easy to imagine how alterations in canonical transcription-associated histone modifications could exacerbate these phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by citation to study proposing this mechanism.
